prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not perturb the clock transition, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B041 with Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements and the chair's summary, the case rests on three things that the discussion has not weakened. First, the central idea is specific and checkable: in a Lamb-Dicke lattice at the magic wavelength the trap light shift cancels for the clock transition, so many neutral atoms can be held and interrogated together without the trap spoiling the measurement. Second, the result is a measured, reproduced outcome and not a forecast: uncertainties near 1e-18 are reached and compared across several independent laboratories, and nobody on the committee has argued that the science is premature. Third, the credit is complete within the two names, with no decisive contributor who must be dropped to respect the three-person limit. I consider this the cleanest attribution among the leading candidates. On the chair's question about the 2005 and 2012 prizes, I think the citation can distinguish them plainly. The comb supplied the means to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize concerned control and measurement of single quantum systems. The lattice clock is a different mechanism, a way of removing the dominant systematic shift while interrogating a large ensemble, and it is the step that opened the 1e-18 regime for neutral atoms. On the redefinition of the second, I would not make the prize depend on it. The physics is established whether or not the metrological bodies adopt a new definition this decade, and waiting would tie a scientific judgment to an administrative timetable. I also want to say plainly that I have not moved because B018 has more first-place support. I would support B018 if the committee concludes after examination that the attribution and precedent questions for B041 cannot be answered, but I do not think that is the case.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness of B041 is that it is an instrument and a precision-measurement result rather than the discovery of a new phase or phenomenon, and a member who holds to the will's wording strictly can reasonably give that more weight than I do. A citation that speaks mainly about accuracy would invite the incremental-improvement reading; it must name the magic-wavelength lattice and the neutral-atom ensemble as the new element. Ion-clock work, ultrastable lasers and the comb are the enabling toolbox and are not credited, and some will say that this leaves the history incomplete. B018 has the broader opening support and a decades-long stable interpretation, and its science is not in doubt. Finally, I am an atomic physicist and have a personal history near the JILA environment, so I may overweight how hard it was to control systematic shifts in lattice clocks and I should be discounted accordingly on that point.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B018 first as a prediction followed by a clean observation, and asks whether the decisive element of B041 is the lattice scheme itself or the later metrological performance.
responses.response: On your question, I would say that the two cannot be separated in the way the question suggests, and for that reason the citation should name both. The magic-wavelength idea alone was a proposal; what made it a discovery in the sense of the will was that it worked, and that systematic shifts could be controlled to 1e-18 with large atom numbers. That is why I credit Katori for the concept and Ye for the highest-performing realizations and not either one alone. I do accept your point that B018 has a clear logical structure of prediction followed by observation, and I do not think B041 beats it on that criterion. Where I differ is that I do not see the attribution of B018 as equally clean: you and the others in your camp all concede that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the trio, and that Zhang cannot be honoured. A narrow quantum spin Hall citation helps, but it does not remove the fact that the experiment followed a proposal from people the prize would not name.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B016 to B018 and lists B041 first among alternatives; he calls the clock close to his idea of an experimental achievement but worries about the pending redefinition of the second and the earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: I appreciate that you hold B041 as your first alternative, and I think that makes the real question the one you posed: which criterion decides. For me it is completeness of attribution together with maturity, because those are the two criteria where a committee has the least room for later regret. On the redefinition, I would answer that a prize for the lattice clock does not need the redefinition to be adopted; the evidence is the agreement of independent clocks, and that exists today. If the committee waits, it is waiting on a decision about the second that the physics already supports. I would ask you whether your hesitation is about the science or only about the timing of an external body, because if it is only timing, I think it should not carry weight.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B041 from B020 after disclosing a conflict, says that earlier prizes in 2005 and 2012 oblige the committee to state what is new, and would fall back on B018 if a convincing lattice-clock citation cannot be written.
responses.response: I agree with the test you set, and I think it can be met. The new element is that neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice carry no first-order light shift on the clock transition, which is what allows a very large number of atoms to be interrogated at once, and that is what gives the statistical advantage at 1e-18. I have drafted the citation to say exactly that and to avoid the generic word accuracy. I also thank you for the disclosure on B020 and for handling it by changing your position; I think the committee should treat the B020 question as closed for this year, given the four-for-three problem and the 2025 prize. If the committee fails to write a clock citation that you find convincing, I would accept your fallback to B018, and I would rather we reach it by that route than by counting first places.

responses.point: Eriksson moved his lead to B018 after the opening ballots, accepts the incompleteness of the history (Zhang deceased, Bernevig and Hughes uncredited), and says he defers to Kroll and Lindroth on the physics of B041 because it lies outside his field.
responses.response: Thank you for the deference, but I would not want it to substitute for a judgment, because the question of whether a measurement platform counts as a discovery is exactly one that a theorist can assess. You argue that the conceptual reach of topological band theory is larger, and I accept that as a real consideration, as a measure of breadth. I would ask in return whether breadth should outweigh a fully clean attribution. You have said that the history behind B018 is incomplete, and that the committee should say so openly in deliberation. A prize whose citation has to be defended with a statement of who is not credited is a more fragile result than one whose two names are the people the field itself would name. On your own earlier doubt about B009, I note that we agree a method whose accuracy depends on solver choices is a weaker candidate.

responses.point: Olsson holds B018 first as the clearest example of a discovery with an identifiable origin and experimental confirmation, and in round 1 put the clock fourth because it lies outside her field and she considers the incrementality worry less decisive than the field-distance.
responses.response: I understand that your reservation about B041 is distance from the field and not scepticism about the result, and I think that is a fair and honest account. You describe B018 as the example of origin plus confirmation; I would say that B041 also has an identifiable origin, the magic-wavelength proposal, and an identifiable confirmation, the strontium lattice clocks that followed, and then the large improvement in performance. I also take your point that your own opinion on B020 should not be counted as independent from Johansson's. I would add that the same discipline applies to me on B041, which is why I put my own conflict note first and ask the committee to weigh my statement with that in mind.

uncertainties: Whether the committee finds a lattice-clock citation sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 individual-quantum-system prizes; I think it can, but I am one of the three members for whom this is a home field and others may judge differently.
Whether a prize for an instrument and its performance counts as a discovery in the sense of the will; this is a difference in interpretation that I cannot resolve with evidence in the file.
Whether the contributions of ultrastable lasers and ion-clock work should be reflected in the citation or in the credited names. I would handle it in the wording and not by adding a third name.
Priority details for the first magic-wavelength proposal and the earliest demonstrations are from my memory and should be checked against the primary papers before the final text is fixed.
For B018, I cannot settle from the file whether the 2016 prize leaves room, or whether a narrow quantum spin Hall citation survives the priority claims for 3D topological insulators.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. During my doctoral period I did a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is associated with the JILA environment in which Jun Ye works. That stay is decades old, I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I regard it as a possible connection for the committee to judge and not as a conflict that requires recusal. My own field, atomic physics and laser stabilisation at Lund, gives me professional familiarity with the subject of B041, which I disclose so that my judgment of the metrology case can be discounted for home-field bias. I have no documented connection to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp (B018) or to the credited names of B010. I note that I proposed B010 only as an alternative, and that my own work on quantum memories and optical quantum information is adjacent to, but not part of, B010 and B028.
